title: What Identities Warrant the Lens of Intersectionality in Psychology and Human Development Research?: A Comprehensive Literature Review
abstract: Coined by legal scholar Kimberlé Crenshaw in 1989, intersectionality is a paradigm for understanding how individuals’ multiple identities converge. Although intersectionality has long been used by sociologists and ethnic studies scholars, it has only recently been taken up by psychologists as an analytic tool for understanding identity. This project is a substudy of an ongoing systematic literature review intending to identify and analyze how intersectionality is defined and measured in psychological research on identity processes. In particular, we aim to identify which identities psychologists are examining through the lens of intersectionality. We collected texts (n=1361) from PsycInfo, a leading database of psychological scholarship. Next, we conducted inclusion coding to select US-based empirical research focusing on identity processes, resulting in a final yield of 359 peer-reviewed articles (n=167), dissertations (n=179), and book chapters (n=11). Using NVivo 12, we content coded all remaining texts for sample demographics, methodologies used, and identities studied. Our discovery-based process resulted in a much more diverse list of identity categories than expected based on the foundational race/class/gender focus of intersectionality. Although many texts focus on racial-ethnic (n=307), gender (n=297), sexual (n=135), and class (n=91) identities, the presence of other categories (i.e., work, religious, and immigrant identities) in at least 30 texts each was a particularly interesting finding. The breadth of identities studied indicates that intersectionality is being applied in a range of ways, highlighting the need to examine how intersectionality is being operationalized across disciplines.
